utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-95-12-PT, the Prosecutor of the Tribunal against Ivica Rajic, also known as Viktor Andric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, may we have the appearances, please. For the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Good afternoon. Kenneth Scott for the Prosecution. With me is trial attorney Josee D'Aoust, and our case manager, of course, Skye Winner. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KOSTA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Co-counsel Doris Kosta appearing for Mr. Ivica Rajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. Well, Mr. Rajic, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you have anything to complain at this stage?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not at this stage, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Well, good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. This Trial Chamber is seized of the filing of documents relating to Rule 62 ter filed jointly by the Prosecution and the Defence dated the 25th October 2005. Two documents and several annexes attached to this motion which are the plea agreement and the factual basis. First of all, we would like to ask the parties to brief us on those documents first, and after that, the Judges might have some questions to those parties. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May it please the Court, Mr. President, you're correct. Two documents have been filed in connection with today's hearing. One is a document titled Plea Agreement. Another document is titled Factual Basis. Those documents, of course, have been non-public up until this moment, but now that the hearing has begun we would -- by joint agreement with the Defence, we would ask that those documents be released to the public with the important exception, please, of confidential Annex 3. But with the exception of Annex 3, all of these documents may now be, with the Court's permission, released to the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Could I turn to the Defence. Any objections to that? Madam Kosta.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KOSTA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, no objections to what the Prosecutor has just put forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we have decided to lift the confidentiality of the documents except the Annex 3. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, the Prosecution will provide the Chamber with a brief summary of the plea agreement, and I know the Chamber has that of course in front of you, but I will touch upon what might be considered the most important or operative elements. I should say at the outset for the record, purposes of the record, that both of these documents, the plea agreement and the factual basis, have also been fully prepared in the B/C/S or Croatian language and available and of course carefully reviewed by the accused and counsel. The plea agreement document, Your Honours, sets out the parties' entire agreement. That is, there are no other agreements. There are no so-called side agreements or nothing, no promises or suggestions on the side apart from the agreements on the face of this document which the Chamber has before it. The plea agreement includes a waiver of various rights by the accused, the right to remain silent, the right to plead not guilty and require the Prosecution to prove its charges beyond and reasonable doubt, the right to prepare and put forward a defence, the right to defend himself in person or through legal assistance of counsel, the right to examine at his trial or have examined the witnesses against him, and of course the right not to be compelled to testify against himself. The accused has waived these rights in going forward and presenting this guilty plea agreement to Your Honours for your consideration. The plea agreement involves the accused pleading guilty to four counts of the amended indictment. An amended indictment was filed with the Court's permission on the 14th of January, 2004. Under the plea agreement, the accused will plead guilty to: Count 1, wilful killing, a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions; Count 3 inhuman treatment, including sexual assault, a grave breach of Geneva Conventions; Count 7, appropriation of property, a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions; and, finally, Count 9, extensive destruction not justified by military necessity and carried out unlawful and wantonly, a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions. As an integral part of the plea agreement, a written factual basis has been prepared which actually is the second document but which is also incorporated in and part of the plea agreement itself. We will come to that document, I'm sure, as this hearing continues, and I will put off the discussion of that document until a further stage. In summary, if I can say, Your Honours, in summary the facts -- the factual basis sets out that the accused Ivica Rajic is pleading guilty to the charges because he is guilty and he accepts responsibility for the actions and omissions that are charged as crimes in the amended indictment. The plea agreement also advises or informs the accused of the fundamental law under Articles 7(1) and 7(3) of the Tribunal Statute and what the Prosecution would be required to prove in order to obtain convictions related to either Article 7(1) and/or Article 7(3). The plea agreement also sets out, so that the accused is fully informed, the elements of each of the crimes to which he is pleading guilty, the crimes that I've just mentioned a moment ago, Count 1, Count 3, Count 7, and Count 9, and the elements of those offences are all set out in the agreement. In terms of sentencing, Your Honours, the Prosecutor and the accused Ivica Rajic agree and will recommend in connection with the pleas of guilty to Counts 1, 3, 7, and 9 a single combined sentence in the range of 12 to 15 years, and under the parties' agreement, the Defence, Mr. Rajic, will be able to argue to this Chamber or to the sentencing Chamber a sentence as low as 12 years and at the same time the Prosecutor is able to, under the plea agreement argue, for a sentence of 15 years. The Prosecutor and Mr. Rajic understand fully, and Mr. Rajic has been informed, that whatever the parties' agreement or recommendation, that of course is not binding on the Chamber. As a further component of the plea agreement, Your Honours, Mr. Rajic agrees to full and substantial cooperation with the Prosecutor, which may involve the giving of truthful testimony in other proceedings. Now, in terms of what the Prosecutor agrees to in exchange, if you will, for Mr. Rajic's guilty pleas and the matters that I've discussed so far, the Prosecutor agrees to the following: Again, to a single combined sentence in the range of 12 to 15 years with the same proviso, the accused can argue for sentence of 12 years, the Prosecution can argue for a sentence of up to 15 years, again with the full understanding that ultimately sentencing, of course, is entirely the discretion of the sentencing Chamber. Further, the Prosecutor agrees that at the time of the Trial Chamber's acceptance of the guilty plea and sentence, the Prosecutor will move to dismiss the remaining counts of the amended indictment without prejudice. The counts, of course, to which Mr. Rajic is not entering a guilty plea. And finally, the Prosecutor will not bring any other ICTY charges against Mr. Rajic except, and I think this is important, except he may be prosecuted for perjury, obstruction of justice or contempt should in the future he be found to be guilty of any of that conduct. Should he appear as a witness in any proceeding and intentionally commit perjury, then there is nothing in this plea agreement that would protect him against prosecution for that. Finally the -- in signing this plea agreement Mr. Rajic makes the following fundamental affirmations: First, his pleas of guilty to Counts 1, 3, 7 and 9 are made voluntarily. Second, the guilty pleas are informed and that Mr. Rajic understands his rights, has been informed of the procedures involved, and is fully informed of the nature and consequences of his guilty pleas. Further, his guilty pleas are not equivocal and he is pleading guilty because he is guilty and for no other reason. Finally, he affirms that there is a sufficient factual basis for the crimes to which he is pleading guilty and to his participation or role in those crimes. And finally, as I said at the outset, the plea agreement further confirms that this is in fact the parties' entire agreement as set forth in this document. And that is the summary, Your Honours, of the plea agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could I now turn to the Defence. Madam Kosta, do you have anything to add or have any observations to make?

utterances.speaker: MS. KOSTA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, now that we have heard the position of the OTP and since the joint filing was also a result of an agreement that we had reached on the points put forward by the OTP, I'm glad to say that we have no objections whatsoever to what has been proposed, and we are fully in agreement with this proposal by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Orie, you may raise some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I have a few questions. First of all, the -- the indictment and the charges brought against the accused are brought under Article 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute. In view of the case law, we will have to determine whether this is -- this responsibility is under -- as a result of the same acts where we have to choose, and I would like to hear from the parties what the Chamber should choose, and I would have an additional question to that as well, or that the responsibility results from not the same actions, in which case there is a possibility for multiple conviction. So therefore, I'd like to hear from the parties. And if the preference would be for Article 7(1), I would like to have a further explanation as to the factual basis for a 7(1) responsibility, because the factual basis underlying the plea agreement and the indictment certainly would allow for a 7(1) responsibility, I would say, but it's not entirely clear what the factual basis for a preference for 7(1) would be. So first question, one or more acts, possibility of multiple convictions; and second, the factual basis for the preference expressed by the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Orie, Your Honours. The factual basis that's set out in the plea agreement and in the second document that we've discussed so far this afternoon would provide a factual basis in the Prosecution's view to conviction under both 7(1) and 7(3), or as Judge Orie mentions, you might say 7(1) and/or 7(3) based upon different acts or different counts of the amended indictment. That is -- I'll talk about that and then I'll come back to Judge Orie's other question. That is, there is nothing in the plea agreement as structured that would prevent the Chamber if it so found to base part of its convictions on some counts on a 7(1) theory and on other counts under 7(3) if the Chamber took a view that that was the appropriate basis. I think the factual basis that is put forth would support either or both theories as do all counts that Mr. Rajic is pleading guilty to. Having said that, it's the Prosecution's view that there is indeed a factual basis, a sufficient factual basis for a 7(1) conviction on all four counts based largely on the -- at least, I should say at least on the substantial likelihood standard of the Blaskic appeals judgement. In the Blaskic appeals judgement, as Your Honours know, the issue of mens rea or state of mind for purposes of Article 7(1) was mentioned, and it was concluded this -- I shouldn't say mentioned, it was extensively of course discussed and analysed, and it was concluded that short of a direct criminal order, if you will, an order that on its face by its very terms is criminal, that the 7(1) standard can also be satisfied in a situation where the accused was aware that the carrying out of his orders, the carrying out of what he had put in motion, if you will, that there was a substantial likelihood that that conduct -- that his orders, that the carrying out of his orders or commands would indeed result in the crimes charged -- ultimately charged in the indictment. On that basis, and I believe in -- very specific that is addressed in paragraph 19 of the factual basis where it says that Mr. Rajic was aware that by ordering HVO commanders and soldiers under his command, and I'll paraphrase, to do these various things, there was a substantial likelihood that the crimes charged in the amended indictment would be committed and nonetheless gave such orders with that awareness in violation of Article 7(1). Of course the Chamber again could pick and choose, if you will. I see nothing in the factual basis or the indictment that would prevent the Chamber from doing that. However, I think that consistent with Tribunal practice if Your Honours were to find at the end of the day that the accused could be convicted on both 7(1) and 7(3) on all counts, then the Tribunal practice appears to be that usually the conviction is then or the sentence is then based upon 7(1). But I think that all options, frankly, are open to the Chamber, although the Prosecution takes the position that there is a sufficient basis for Article 7(1) convictions on each count.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Kosta, would you like to add anything to that or would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MS. KOSTA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as concerns the position put forward by the OTP and in view of the fact that we are here today to reach an agreement based on facts, the Defence will leave it to the Trial Chamber to go through the facts and the evidence to ascertain whether there is any responsibility under Article 7(1) and Article 7(3). We shall endeavour to prove that there is in fact a de facto objective responsibility only under one of those two Articles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And which one then?

utterances.speaker: MS. KOSTA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall try to prove 7(3).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that means that if there's agreement on paragraph 19, I have some difficulties in accepting that at a later stage the Defence would argue that there's no 7(1) responsibility but only 7(3) responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. KOSTA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what I said is that we are meeting here today because of the agreement, the fact that we agreed to both 7(1) and 7(2) [sic]. During the proceedings, we shall be delivering evidence in relation to the facts, and we shall leave the decision to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you finally do accept paragraph 19 that says Mr. Rajic gave his orders in violation of the ICTY's Statute of Article 7(1).

utterances.speaker: MS. KOSTA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the agreement that we signed, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that has been clarified again. I have one other question perhaps for you, Mr. Scott. I did not fully find the time to compare the factual basis with the Appeals Chamber judgement in the Blaskic case. It takes a bit more time to carefully compare them. I take it that you have been involved in the conversations prior to this plea agreement. Would there be any point where you would say that this plea agreement and the factual basis for it would deviate from what the Appeals Chamber has factually established in the Blaskic case, because if that would be the case, we might want to look a bit closer to the material that supports the -- the agreement on the factual basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Of course, yes, I have been closely involved in these matters and discussions for some time, and I would say as -- if I can start by perhaps just an intellectual observation, I think there is an interesting question or issue -- not so much an issue but an interesting question between when failure to prevent under 7(3) becomes substantial likelihood under 7(1), and I suppose there will be cases in the future that perhaps will help us draw that line more clearly, but where it is failure to prevent -- the sufficient knew or should have known and failed to prevent, stop and substantial likelihood begin. But as I say, that's I think an interesting intellectual question for future decisions by either this Chamber, the Appeals Chamber, or what have you. It's the Prosecution position, Judge Orie, Your Honours, in this case that there is sufficient factual basis to satisfy the Blaskic Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. standard as to each of the four counts, that is, to each of these counts the level of this accused's knowledge or awareness - awareness is the actual term - was sufficient to put him on notice as to the four crimes charged in this case which are, of course, wilful killing, inhuman treatment, appropriation of property, and the destruction of property. And as to each of those four counts the Prosecution contents, submits, that there would be sufficient basis under the Blaskic standard basis of those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not only talking about the standard. I'm also talking about the findings, the factual findings in the Blaskic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because the name of Blaskic appears now and then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it could be where he appears -- and, again, I had not yet an opportunity to fully compare. It might contradict the findings so not a standard but contradict the findings, although if it comes to acquittals these findings are usually of a negative character. Is there any such tension between the facts as agreed upon here and the facts established or facts that the Appeals Chamber was not able to establish in the Blaskic case?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I better understand your question now. I don't believe that the factual basis -- that anything in the factual basis is fundamentally inconsistent with the -- if you will, the factual findings, if we can call them that, in the Blaskic appeals judgement. You're right, of course, that Mr. Blaskic's name is mentioned several times but it's primarily by way of background and by way of the chain of command, but there's nothing in the facts -- in the factual basis set out here that would clearly, I would say -- I would emphasise the word clearly so contradict something in the Blaskic appeals judgement to be fundamentally inconsistent. I think one might say that there's some information possibly presented here which in some -- has some general bearing or provide some additional insight into what was happening into Central Bosnia during this time. But having said that, I don't think it's of such a nature that it's inconsistent with the findings in the Blaskic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that would mean that we would not have to pay any -- very specific attention to the factual basis as far as these kinds of facts are concerned. May I ask you, Madam Kosta, whether you would agree with what Mr. Scott just told us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KOSTA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our position is that these proceedings and all other proceedings should be based on properly established facts. I believe that this Trial Chamber should look deeper into the Blaskic issue regardless of the fact that the Prosecution claims that there are no inconsistencies there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that you say the Prosecutor doesn't claim there to be any inconsistencies, but you should look closer to it. Do you have any suggestion, then, that there would be any inconsistencies, and of course we would be greatly assisted if that's the case that you draw our attention to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KOSTA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that at this point the Defence is not ready to point to precise facts, specific facts. However, I have to say that during the Blaskic trial it was precisely my client who through his then attorney expressed a desire to take part in that trial, presumably to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't want to interrupt counsel but if counsel is finished and if your questions, Your Honour, for Ms. Kosta are finished, I would like to clarify because it is an important question, and I don't want the Trial Chamber to feel in any way misled by the Prosecution, of course. Blaskic was not charged with any crimes in Stupni Do so that was not part of the appeals judgement, and therefore that is the basic reason why I say there is nothing in the factual basis that is fundamentally at odds with the Blaskic judgement in this particular respect, so there's no misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, could we regard the plea agreement as well as other issues that you made today as an oral application for the amendment of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not sure what Your Honour means. We don't see it as part of the plea agreement that any part of the indictment needs to be amended. Of course if the Chamber accepts the guilty plea and sentences Mr. Rajic on the four counts, then the Prosecution will indeed move to dismiss the remaining counts, if that's perhaps what Your Honour meant. If not, then I'm in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that the amended indictment shall be filed to the Office of the Registrar as early as possible after this hearing if you want to delete the remaining counts which are not included in the plea agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour. I'm sorry, I'm not -- I'm a little bit -- it was not our intention -- I know in some situations, for example, I know from reading -- I don't think this is a -- just let me consult with counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Out of abundance of caution, I won't mention the names of accused in other cases. But I think I can say that the Chamber may know that in other cases involving plea agreement, part of the plea agreement has involved an amended indictment being specifically prepared for the purposes of the plea. Additional charges not in an existing indictment have been proposed for the accused then to enter his guilty plea to. That's not the situation in case. So the Prosecution does not anticipate -- of course, if the Chamber so directs, we will consider it and look at it further, but the Prosecution in this case does not anticipate bringing any new amended indictment. Mr. Rajic will be pleading guilty to four counts in the existing indictment and we would propose, Your Honour, at the time of sentencing and when the Chamber ultimately accepts the plea, then of course the Chamber -- excuse me, the Prosecution will move to dismiss the remaining counts, if that would be consistent with Your Honour's direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe we could do that at the time of sentencing when the Chamber ultimately accepts the plea. Then the Prosecution will move to dismiss the remaining counts at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. So shall we proceed to the plea of the counts in the indictment. Mr. Rajic, did you have the opportunity to discuss the contents of the plea agreement with your counsel?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, I did have opportunity, and I did discuss with my attorney all of the documents mentioned today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you understand the meaning of each remaining count?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, I understand fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you ready to change your plea at this moment? I mean that you pled to not guilty before, and after the plea agreement are you going to change your original plea?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am prepared to amend my previous pleas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. My suggestion is that I read out each count in the plea agreement, and you may plead guilty or not guilty as the case may be. Are you ready to plead?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's start. How do you plead to Count 1, wilful killing, a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, punishable under at Statute Articles 2(a), 7(1) and 7(3), guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Guilty, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Very well. Count 3, inhuman treatment, including sexual assault, a grave breach to the Geneva Conventions of 1949, punishable under Statute Articles 2(b), 7(1) and 7(3). How do you plead, guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Count 7, appropriation of property, a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, punishable under Statute Article 2(d), 7(1) and 7(3). How do you plead, guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Count 9, extensive destruction not justified by military necessity and carried out unlawfully and wantonly, a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, punishable under Statute Article 2(d), 7(1) and 7(3). How do you plead, guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Guilty, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down, please. The Trial Chamber will record a plea of guilty of the four counts by the accused, Mr. Rajic. Well, Mr. Rajic, since you pleaded guilty to the four counts of the amended indictment, I would like to address the accused, Mr. Rajic, at this stage. Mr. Rajic, the Trial Chamber would like to find out from you whether you understand the details of this plea agreement you entered into with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I was informed about the contents of the documents which were produced together with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I also would like to know that you have entered a guilty plea voluntarily and of out of your free will, which means whether you were threatened or coerced in any way to make this agreement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. I was not threatened. I pleaded guilty because that's what I firmly believe, that indeed I am guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber also would like to know whether your counsel, Madam Kosta, has advised you of the consequences of pleading guilty to the four counts in the amended indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. My counsel has informed me of all potential consequences of pleading guilty to four counts of indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: At this stage, I have to remind you that when you're entering into the plea agreement, you understand that the Trial Chamber is not bound to accept the range of the sentence agreed upon by yourself and the Prosecutor. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that, Your Honours. I hope that the sentence will be a just one, and I do understand that the Trial Chamber is not bound by the sentencing agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that we will have a short break during which the Bench will deliberate on the acceptance of the plea agreement, and we will resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, after the deliberations, we would like to say that the Trial Chamber has considered the particulars of the facts in the plea agreement and is satisfied they do form sufficient factual basis for finding the accused guilty on those counts and, therefore, makes a finding of guilty and enters the conviction for four counts against the accused, Mr. Rajic. The Trial Chamber will now move to the next stage about a possible date for hearings on sentencing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will now move to the next stage about a possible date for hearing on sentencing and would like to find out from both parties how they intend to make their submissions on sentencing. Mr. Scott, would you please indicate how much time you think you need.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I think that we could reasonably prepare a sentence, a written sentencing submission, in approximately two to three weeks. I don't think at this point that we anticipate an extensive submission. Certainly I think it will be something that will be helpful to the Chamber, but I don't think it's going to be something that's extremely voluminous. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. I turn to Defence counsel. Madam Kosta, would you please indicate how much time do you need for the preparation of that brief.

utterances.speaker: MS. KOSTA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the preparation of the Defence brief, I believe that I would need up to three weeks for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, after consultations with my colleagues, we believe that the 15th of November for filing of the sentencing brief, and the sentence hearing will be sometime at the end of November, maybe on the 28th of November. The Trial Chamber will issue orders relating to the further proceedings in due course. Are there any other matters that the parties would like to bring to the attention of this Bench. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Not from the Prosecution, Your Honour. We appreciate the Chamber's attention this afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence, Madam Kosta.

utterances.speaker: MS. KOSTA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Likewise we have no suggestions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Rajic, do you want to say something at this stage?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at the conclusion I would like to put in a request. This has to do with the status of my former counsel, Mr. Zeljko Olujic, who I dismissed from the case because he obstructed on purpose the preparation of my defence and as well as my cooperation with the Prosecution in order to establish the truth. In view of the fact that from that date on, from the date when I dismissed Mr. Olujic, he continues to appear as my Defence counsel publicly. This is something that affects adversely my status and my cooperation with this Tribunal. Therefore, I would like to ask the Trial Chamber to do something to discontinue sending of any documents to Mr. Olujic, because I'm convinced that these documents end up in the wrong hands, in the hands of the people who are working against me, against justice, and against this Tribunal. That's all I wanted to say, because -- I simply wanted to draw your attention to the fact that he is a common thief and fraudster. That's all I have to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, that is a very serious allegation, Mr. Rajic, but anyway, we will convey your statement to the Registrar. And I found that from the latest filings Mr. Olujic's name does not appear on the documents. I guess that he will no longer get any documents of this case from now on. But anyway, we will draw the attention of the Registrar to this matter. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe that's all for this hearing. The hearing is adjourned.
